text:
### Observed differences

- Six activities became near-universal. In the earlier window, A28, A30 and A31 each appeared in about 49 in 100 cases, and A32, A33 and A34 in about 52 in 100; in the later window, each of the six appears in about 99–100 in 100 cases. None of them repeats within a case in either window (mean occurrences per trace equals participation throughout). [OCC001, OCC002, OCC003, OCC004, OCC005, OCC006]

- The two groups of three were mutually exclusive alternatives and now run together. In the earlier window, cross-group pairs such as A28–A32, A30–A33 or A31–A34 never shared a case (0 in 100; every case contained exactly one of the two activities), while within each group the three activities always appeared together. In the later window, cross-group pairs co-occur in about 98 in 100 cases, and whenever they do, the A28/A30/A31 member comes first. [REL015, REL016, REL017, REL019, REL020, REL021, REL022, REL023, REL024, REL013]

- Routing moved with this. From A25, transitions into the A28/A30/A31 group rose from about 49 in 100 observed outgoing transitions to about 99 in 100, while transitions into A32/A33/A34 fell from about 52 in 100 to about 1 in 100. From A28, A30 and A31, the direct edge to A26 (about 30–36 in 100) nearly disappeared (about 0.5 in 100), replaced by edges to A32, A33 and A34 (about 10–13 in 100 each). [DIR001, DIR002, DIR003, DIR004]

- Event distances are consistent with the second group now sitting between the first group and A26: the pairs A25–A32/A33/A34, which were 1–3 event positions apart in the earlier window (roughly 30/36/34 in 100), are now 4–5 positions apart (roughly 50/48 in 100); the distance from A28/A30/A31 to A26 shifted the same way, from 1–3 to 4–5 positions. [LAG001, LAG002, LAG003, LAG004, LAG005, LAG006]

- Relative positions shifted slightly (A25 and the A28/A30/A31 group a little earlier, A26 and A32/A33/A34 a little later; e.g., A25 mean relative position 0.67 to 0.62, A26 0.80 to 0.83), and within each group both orders still occur in similar proportions in both windows, so neither group has a fixed internal order before or after. A25 and A26 occur in every case in both windows. [POS001, POS002, POS003, POS004, POS005, POS006, POS007, POS008, REL025, REL026, REL027]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the hypothesis that the exclusive choice between the two activity groups was replaced by sequential execution of both: in the earlier window a case ran either {A28, A30, A31} or {A32, A33, A34} (roughly fifty-fifty, never both), whereas in the later window a case typically runs A25, then A28/A30/A31 in no fixed internal order, then A32/A33/A34 in no fixed internal order, then A26 — the second group is no longer skipped when the first runs. The change is shown directly by the relational items (cross-group co-occurrence from 0 to about 98 in 100, always in the same cross-group order) and is consistent across the participation items (all six activities rising from about half of cases to nearly all), the routing items (A25 now enters the first group; the first group now leads to the second instead of to A26) and the distance items (the second group and A26 now sit 4–5 event positions after their predecessors instead of 1–3). With 51 qualifying items against about 0.59 expected by chance among the 118 tested units, sampling noise cannot account for the pattern as a whole. [REL015, REL019, REL022, OCC001, OCC004, DIR001, DIR002, LAG001, LAG004]

Limitations: the evidence contains no outgoing-transition profile for A32, A33 or A34, so the return from the second group to A26 is inferred from order relations (the second group precedes A26 in about 99–100 in 100 cases) rather than from observed edges. An important competing explanation the evidence cannot fully rule out concerns the roughly 1–2 in 100 later cases that still contain only one of the two groups: it cannot show whether these are remnants of the old exclusive behaviour or ordinary variation. [REL010, REL011, REL012, REL013, OCC001]
